doc.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025

title: Classical piano lessons, church family and doo-wop
summary: Piano lessons at Wurlitzer, copying Horace Silver, a musical church family, and growing up on R&B and doo-wop.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Were you playing — the piano you were playing at the time, was it classical music or were you learning chords and trying to copy jazz pianists? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

I was. I was, you know I was taking classical lessons, like I say my mother started me at the Wurtlitzer School of Music in downtown Buffalo when I was about eight. And they had a deal going that if you bought a new piano you got a year or two of free lessons with the piano. So me and my big sister, we both availed ourself, and we’d go for lessons. And then after that ran out then my mother hired a piano teacher who came by the house you know. And so we were doing all the regular you know piano primer books, but I always had my ear on what was going on at the time, the doo-wop, the soul, and when I got in high school my jazz ear got opened. And so I had a few — and there were a few pianists that I thought I could copy, like Horace Silver and Bobby Timmons, the blues oriented guys. So I started teaching myself how to do that. And so I was kind of doing both at the same time.

I just was reading a book about early rock & roll and the chitlin’ circuit and how popular guys like Roy Brown were at the time in the mid-50s. I’m wondering if that music, which was — we used to think of it was pre-rock & roll, or R&B, was that something you listened to? And also I wonder what did your parents like having played in the house? What kind of music?

Well first of all people will ask me what drew me to the bass and I tell them I used to spend, my father sang bass in the choir at the church. And as a little guy I used to stand next to him while he was rolling out these luscious bass notes, you know, in the choir. And so the church was full of family members who were involved in music. My aunt played the organ, directed the choir. I had another uncle who was a baritone soloist. He used to do solo concerts. And my cousins, you know they all play. So we just had a rich musical — and my mother even played. My mother played — she said the whole nine months she was carrying me she was playing in her mother’s church. Her mother was an evangelist and so she was playing and directing the choir. And she was wishing that I might be a musician. And later on when I started traveling the globe as a musician she said, “You have to be careful what you pray for.”

Be careful what you ask for — what you pray for, you know, ‘cause it may come back to haunt you. Because I was never at home. But no, yeah, we were very much affect— and see the other thing about those days is that there was only a couple of radio stations and you had race record stores and you had what they called race records — I mean radio stations. And so we were all in the ‘50s pretty much listening to the same music, you know, the popular music of the time you know. We knew as much about the black R&B artisans as we did about the white ones you know. Because you’d get a little bit of both. They’d mix it up a lot. You know Benny & the Jets and James Brown and the Cadillacs and all these old people. So we grew up on doo-wop basically. Which is basically various © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

forms of blues. And so I guess we started out imitating those sounds and those chords on the piano, which is a lot of repetition. [scats] So we kind of taught ourselves how to — nobody ever really taught us how to do that, we kind of figured it out.
